# The ordinary Fueter Hardy space and limits of discrete series

**R060, 2026-10-17.** This sharpens the endpoint in [the corrected realization](corrected-realization.md#8-what-happens-for-ordinary-quaternion-valued-functions). Ordinary quaternion-valued Fueter functions, with a Hardy boundary condition, realize a genuine limit of discrete series of $G=\operatorname{Sp}(1,1)\simeq\operatorname{Spin}_0(4,1)$. They are one of the two irreducible summands of the spinor principal series at normalized parameter zero. The adjective “limit” has its representation-theoretic meaning here; it is not merely a suggestion based on the divergent Bergman integral.

**Evidence.** The boundary realization and splitting below are supplied arguments extending the previous proof. The classification as limits of discrete series is supported by Liu–Zhang, printed p. 2996 after Theorem 3.11, and Camporesi–Pedon, *Harmonic analysis for spinors on real hyperbolic spaces*, printed pp. 250–252, especially the final step of Theorem 3.2. The latter explicitly corrects an earlier mistaken classification as discrete series. No independent review or Lean verification is claimed.

## 1. The representation and its Hilbert condition

Use $q=t+ix+jy+kz$, $D_l=\partial_t+i\partial_x+j\partial_y+k\partial_z$, and right complex scalars in $\mathbb H$. Let $d\sigma$ be probability area on $S^3$. Define
$$
\mathscr H_+=\left\{h:B\to\mathbb H:D_lh=0,\quad
\|h\|^2=\sup_{r<1}\int_{S^3}|h(r\omega)|^2d\sigma(\omega)<\infty\right\}.
$$
For $\gamma^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, set
$$
q'=(aq+b)(cq+d)^{-1},\qquad J=cq+d,
\qquad (\Pi(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q'). \tag{H1}
$$
The [previous proof](corrected-realization.md) establishes covariance, unitarity, irreducibility, and
$$
\mathscr H_+|_K=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m\ge0}V_m\boxtimes V_{m+1},
\qquad K=\operatorname{Sp}(1)_L\times\operatorname{Sp}(1)_R. \tag{H2}
$$
Here $V_m=\operatorname{Sym}^m\mathbb C^2$. The boundary trace is isometric onto the closure of regular polynomials in $L^2(S^3,\mathbb H)$. This follows from the orthogonal homogeneous harmonic expansion: the boundary norm is the sum of squared homogeneous norms and the radial norm inserts factors $r^{2m}$.

The theorem concerns this Hilbert space, not every regular function without a boundary growth condition. The central element $-I\in G$ acts by $-1$ in (H1), so this representation needs the spin group and does not descend to $\operatorname{SO}_0(4,1)$.

## 2. The normalized principal series and its splitting

Formula (H1) also defines a unitary action on all of
$$
\mathscr B=L^2(S^3,\mathbb H).
$$
The boundary Jacobian is $|J|^{-6}$ and the multiplier has squared norm $|J|^{-6}$. Let $P=MAN$ stabilize $1\in S^3$. Then $M\simeq\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ is the diagonal subgroup of $K$, and its action on the fibre at $1$ is its standard complex two-dimensional representation $\sigma=V_1$.

With $a_t=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh(t/2)&\sinh(t/2)\\\sinh(t/2)&\cosh(t/2)\end{pmatrix}$, the positive restricted root has value $t$ and $\rho=3/2$. Thus this boundary action is
$$
I(\sigma,0)=\operatorname{Ind}_{MAN}^{G}(\sigma\otimes1\otimes1)
\tag{H3}
$$
in **normalized** induction. In the usual induced-section convention, $F(gma_tn)=e^{-3t/2}\sigma(m)^{-1}F(g)$. In particular the unnormalized character is not zero. At the fixed point $1$, (H1) gives the inverse-character factor $e^{3t/2}$ for $\Pi(a_t)$, as required.

Peter–Weyl on $S^3\simeq\operatorname{Sp}(1)$ and Clebsch–Gordan give
$$
\mathscr B|_K=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m\ge0}
\left[(V_m\boxtimes V_{m+1})\oplus(V_{m+1}\boxtimes V_m)\right]. \tag{H4}
$$
The two summands can be separated explicitly by the unitary Kelvin involution
$$
(Cf)(\omega)=\bar\omega f(\bar\omega),\qquad C^2=1.
$$
For $k=(a,b)$, $C\Pi(a,b)C=\Pi(b,a)$. More generally
$$
C\Pi(g)C=\Pi(WgW),\qquad W=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}. \tag{H5}
$$
Although $W$ reverses the defining Hermitian form, conjugation by it preserves $G$. Equation (H5) follows by inserting (H1), using $|q|=1$ and $|aq+b|=|cq+d|$ on the boundary. In particular $C\mathscr H_+$ is invariant and irreducible, with the compact factors exchanged. Equations (H2) and (H4) imply the orthogonal decomposition
$$
\boxed{I(\sigma,0)=\mathscr H_+\widehat\oplus\mathscr H_-,\qquad
\mathscr H_-=C\mathscr H_+,\quad
\mathscr H_-|_K=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m\ge0}V_{m+1}\boxtimes V_m.} \tag{H6}
$$
The second summand is the boundary space of exterior regular functions decaying at infinity, via Kelvin transformation. The two inequivalent irreducible summands are the two spinor limits of discrete series identified in the cited literature. This is the precise analogue of the positive/negative Hardy splitting at the weight-one endpoint for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ (with the appropriate group-cover convention there).

## 3. Why the endpoint is not discrete series

Write $s=1-|q|^2$. The lift of a constant vector on the ball has size $s^{3/2}$ on the standard section, whereas $G/K$ has invariant measure proportional to $s^{-4}dv$. Averaging the absolute $p$th power of its nonzero constant-vector matrix coefficient over the compact fibre gives a positive constant times
$$
\int_Bs^{3p/2-4}dv.
$$
This is finite exactly when $p>2$. In particular these coefficients are not in $L^2(G)$. The attempted ball norm with density $s^{-1}dv$ also has no nonzero regular vectors, by monotonicity of spherical square means. The Hardy condition provides the correct nonzero Hilbert realization.

## 4. Relation to the elliptic coefficients

The same Cauchy–Fueter kernel appears in the elliptic construction, but a periodic meromorphic function with poles is not thereby a vector of $\mathscr H_+$. Furthermore general Möbius transformations do not preserve translation lattices. The coefficient sums vary on the space of lattices and have a separate $\mathrm{SL}_4$ Eisenstein realization, developed in [R061](../R061/elliptic-coefficients.md). A correspondence between the two representations would require an additional construction; sharing a kernel does not establish one.

## Sources and coverage

- Liu–Zhang, [retained PDF](../../sources/liu-zhang-quaternionic-discrete-series-2012.pdf), p. 2996 after Theorem 3.11: the $\mathcal H_1$ endpoint is identified as the limit $\pi_1$.
- Roberto Camporesi and Emmanuel Pedon, *Harmonic analysis for spinors on real hyperbolic spaces*, Colloq. Math. **87** (2001), 245–286, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.4064/cm87-2-10), [retained publisher PDF](../../sources/camporesi-pedon-hyperbolic-spinors-2001.pdf). Inspected the opening conventions, principal series normalization, Lemma 3.1, and Theorem 3.2/proof, printed pp. 245–252 (PDF pp. 1–8). Its reference to Thieleker's classification has not been independently audited. The boundary splitting (H6) is proved here rather than attributed to a formula not located in that paper.

What happens for ordinary quaternion-valued functions

For $n=1$, $W_1=\mathbb H$ and the algebraic constraint is empty. The natural action is the usual conformal Fueter action
$$
(\Pi_1(\gamma)h)(q)=|J|^{-2}J^{-1}h(q').
\tag{C18}
$$
Its multiplier has norm $|J|^{-3}$. The corresponding invariant ball norm would use $s^{-1}dv$, but no nonzero regular function has finite such norm. Indeed its spherical square mean $M(r)$ is nondecreasing, since its components are harmonic and $|h|^2$ is subharmonic. For any nonzero $h$, $M(r_0)>0$ for some $r_0$, so
$$
\int_{r_0}^1\frac{M(r)r^3}{1-r^2}\,dr=\infty.
$$
Instead use the Hardy norm
$$
\|h\|_{\mathrm{Hardy}}^2
=\sup_{0<r<1}\int_{S^3}|h(r\omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\omega),
$$
with normalized boundary area. The boundary Jacobian of the Möbius map is $|J|^{-6}$, exactly matching the squared norm of the multiplier in (C18). This yields a unitary action on boundary values. One can first check it on regular polynomials and their translates, then extend by density; their homogeneous expansion identifies this boundary closure with the displayed Hardy space. The same compact averaging proof gives irreducibility, and the compact types are $V_m\boxtimes V_{m+1}$.

This endpoint is not discrete series. For a constant vector, the lift has size $s^{3/2}$ on the section. Averaging the squared constant-vector matrix coefficient over $K$ leaves a positive constant times $s^3$. Its integral against $s^{-4}dv$ diverges. A discrete-series representation has square-integrable matrix coefficients for these vectors, so this excludes that possibility. Liu–Zhang identify this as their limit $\pi_1$ immediately after Theorem 3.11. The [endpoint follow-up](hardy-endpoint.md) proves the splitting of the normalized spinor principal series at zero into this Hardy space and its Kelvin counterpart, and records the genuine limit-of-discrete-series identification.

Thus the holomorphic analogy is valid at the level of a family of first-order equations and weighted function spaces. In the quaternionic case, the higher members require symmetric spinor values, equivalently the compatible tuples of ordinary Fueter-regular functions above. Changing only the volume weight on unrestricted single quaternion-valued functions does not produce this family with its natural action.
